answer: As stated in [S2], commercial banks must additionally consider 'other UNSCRs' and 'lists in the first schedule and the fourth schedule of UAPA, 1967' for sanctions compliance. These refer to other United Nations Security Council resolutions and specific domestic schedules under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, required for implementation of section 51A of the UAPA and section 12A of the WMD Act. [S2] explicitly lists these as additional requirements beyond those previously outlined.

According to [S1], commercial banks must ensure adherence to the provisions of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010, and the Rules made thereunder. Furthermore, they must ensure meticulous compliance with any instructions or communications issued from time to time by the RBI, based on advice received from the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India.

According to [S1], commercial banks must review their money laundering and terrorist financing risk assessment at least annually. [S1] explicitly states: "However, the bank shall review it at least annually."

[S1] states that the bank shall temporarily cease operations in the account until the customer submits the PAN or equivalent e-document thereof or Form No. 60. Before temporarily ceasing operations, the bank shall give the customer an accessible notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard, and include appropriate relaxations in its internal policy for customers unable to provide the documents due to injury, illness, or old age, subject to enhanced monitoring.

According to [S4], a commercial bank must monitor the 'at par' cheque facility offered to co-operative banks and review the arrangements to assess credit risk and reputational risk. Furthermore, [S4] states that the bank retains the right to verify records maintained by co-operative banks/societies for compliance with KYC and AML instructions.

As per [S1], any remittance of funds by way of demand draft, mail/telegraphic transfer, NEFT, IMPS, or any other mode, and issue of travellers’ cheques for value of ₹50,000 and above shall be effected by debit to the customer’s account or against cheques and not against cash payment.

According to [S1] paragraph 61(1), a commercial bank should consider the FATF Statements circulated by the RBI from time to time and publicly available information for identifying countries that do not or insufficiently apply the FATF Recommendations.

Under the general restriction, a commercial bank must collect account payee cheques only for the payee constituent. [S1] states: "The bank shall not collect account payee cheques for any person other than the payee constituent." This means the payee constituent is the sole party for whom collection is permitted under the regulation.

[S1] states that the bank shall undertake countermeasures when called upon so to do by any international or intergovernmental organisation of which India is a member and which is accepted by the Central Government.

For a commercial bank, RBI's KYC requirements operate in addition to, rather than replace, obligations under other laws and regulations. Passage [S1] explicitly states that banks must carry out customer due diligence processes "in addition to" ensuring compliance with the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002 and the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA). This "in addition to and not in substitution of" principle is consistent across multiple RBI directions, indicating that KYC requirements supplement rather than supersede other regulatory obligations.

Yes, according to [S1] paragraph 26, a commercial bank may undertake V-CIP for CDD in case of new customer onboarding for individual customers, as well as for Beneficial Owners (BOs) in case of Legal Entity (LE) customers.
Under the RBI KYC Directions for Commercial Banks, para 31, the bank must obtain any two of the listed documents as proof of business/activity for a sole proprietary firm. [S1], para 31.

When a commercial bank opens a savings bank account for an SHG, it is not required to perform customer due diligence on every member, as [S1] states that the CDD of all the office bearers shall suffice. Therefore, only the due diligence of the office bearers is sufficient for account opening.
According to [S1], a commercial bank must categorise customers into low, medium, and high-risk categories based on its assessment and risk perception.

As per [S3] para 41(1), commercial banks must re-check the risk ratings assigned to customer accounts at least once every six months. The RBI KYC Directions mandate a periodic review of risk categorisation of accounts with such periodicity being at least once in every six months.
A commercial bank must disclose full-fledged information on its products and their implications to customers so they can make an informed judgment about their choice of products. [S1]

A commercial bank must establish a transparent policy for renewing overdue term deposits, which must be non-discretionary and non-discriminatory. The terms and conditions of renewal, including interest rates, must be notified to the customer at the time of acceptance of the deposit. [S1]

The RBI (Commercial Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 do not override or replace other existing laws or regulations applicable to commercial banks. As stated in para 466 [S5], the provisions of these Directions "shall be in addition to, and not in derogation of the provisions of any other laws, rules, regulations, or directions, for the time being in force."

[S1] states that the bank shall make available all printed material used by retail customers, including account opening forms, pay-in-slips, and passbooks, in trilingual form: English, Hindi, and the concerned Regional Language.

Per [S1], a commercial bank must ensure that necessary infrastructure and facilities are put in place and appropriate security measures are taken at each branch where loans are sanctioned against gold or silver collateral. The bank must also ensure that such collateral is handled only within its branches and only by its employees.

The interest rates on deposit accounts and related matters for commercial banks are governed by the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025, as established in [S2], confirmed in [S1] that banks must be guided by them, and clarified in [S4] that these 2025 Directions supersede all prior related instructions.
According to [S1], the bank should periodically organise Exporters' Meet at centres with concentration of exporters to facilitate interaction between the bank and exporters.

According to [S1], a commercial bank's policy must cover auction-related conduct aspects including the auction procedure specifying the trigger event and notice timeline [S1](3), the notice period allowed to borrower(s)/legal heir(s) for loan settlement before auction [S1](5), the empanelment of auctioneers [S1](6), and procedures for loss, deterioration, or discrepancy of collateral with fair compensation and timelines [S1](7). Additionally, [S5] requires that a bank declare a reserve price for the gold and silver collateral at auction, which shall not be less than 90 per cent of its current value, or 85 per cent if auctions fail twice.

According to [S1], a bank may provide additional facilities beyond the minimum BSBD account services, with or without charges, in a non-discretionary and non-discriminatory manner with transparent disclosure to the customer, provided the customer is not required to maintain a minimum balance. The availment of such additional facilities shall be strictly at the option of the customer.
According to [S1] para 192, the bank must undertake at least an annual review of accounts where there has been no customer-induced transaction for more than a year.

According to [S2], banks should give publicity in branches cautioning against dubious deposit schemes. [S1] adds that such messages may be displayed in bank branches (in the state's official language) and at ATMs or Business Correspondent Points for wider customer visibility.

Yes, a commercial bank is held responsible for the conduct of recovery agents it engages. [S1] explicitly states that "The bank, as principal, is responsible for the actions of its agents." [S4] further reinforces this by requiring the bank to ensure agents adhere to instructions and maintain due diligence processes during recovery.
As stated in [S1], a bank shall have "Enquiry" or "May I Help You" counters located near the entry point of the banking hall at all branches, excluding very small branches.
According to [S1], the prescribed post-shipment interest rate ceases from the date of credit to the 'Nostro' account.

As stated in [S1], the bank shall undertake special drives periodically to find out the whereabouts of the customers, their nominees or legal heirs in respect of inoperative accounts / unclaimed deposits.

A commercial bank must conduct regular audits of its outsourced service providers, including subcontractors, which may be performed by its internal or external auditors [S1]. These audits shall assess the service provider's performance, risk management practices, and compliance with laws and regulations, with frequency determined by the nature and extent of risk [S3]. The bank also retains the right to conduct audits and obtain relevant audit reports from the service provider [S4].

According to [S1], when a commercial bank appoints a group entity to perform outsourced services, the selection shall be based on objective reasons that are similar to the selection of a third-party, and the bank must appropriately deal with any conflicts of interest that such an arrangement may entail.

Per [S1], an NBFC bears responsibility for the conduct of DSAs/DMAs and recovery agents engaged through a service provider. Per [S2], a bank bears similar responsibility for such agents, as both retain ultimate control and are accountable for their actions and customer information confidentiality.

[S1] (para 54) states that a commercial bank must ensure a non-group service provider is not owned or controlled by any director, key managerial personnel, approver of the outsourcing arrangement, or their relatives. [S4] (para 18)(v) similarly prohibits such ownership or control for service providers that are not subsidiaries of the bank. An exception may be permitted only with the approval of the Board or a Committee of the Board, followed by appropriate disclosure, oversight, and monitoring, as provided in the proviso to [S1] and referenced in [S3] (para 13)(iv).

[S1] paragraph 65 states that sufficient compliance requires clear separation and isolation of the bank's data from its customers' specific data and information, ensuring only authorised bank personnel can access their respective data in a multi-tenant environment/architecture.

Yes, according to [S2], outsourcing arrangements "shall not affect the rights of its customers against the bank, including the ability of the customers to obtain redressal as applicable under relevant laws." [S3] further states that "responsibility for redressal of customers’ grievances related to outsourced services shall rest with the bank."
Under the RBI's 2025 outsourcing directions, commercial banks must include in their outsourcing agreements a clause granting the right to conduct audits

Yes, a commercial bank may outsource any IT service within its business group or conglomerate, provided that such an arrangement is backed by the Board-approved policy and appropriate SLAs / agreements with its group entities are in place. [S1]

[S1] explicitly allows commercial banks (as REs) to adopt a pooled (shared) audit when multiple REs use the same third-party IT service provider, instead of conducting separate audits. However, the REs remain responsible for ensuring that audit requirements related to their respective contracts with the service provider are met effectively. The passage states that REs can either pool their audit resources or engage an independent third-party auditor to jointly audit a common service provider.

According to paragraph 66 of the Commercial Banks directions, a bank must consider additional factors when evaluating a service provider for outsourced IT services, including technology and infrastructural stability, data backup and disaster recovery plans, conflict of interest, the provider’s capability to identify and segregate the bank’s data, information/cyber security risk assessment, appropriate controls and contractual arrangements for data protection and the bank’s access to data, the ability to service customers confidentially across multiple entities, and the ability to enforce agreements regarding data storage, protection, and confidentiality [S1].

Under [S1] paragraph 77, a commercial bank must create an inventory of IT services outsourced to service providers, including key entities involved in their supply chains. This inventory is a core requirement under the RBI's outsourcing risk management directions for commercial banks.

As stated in [S1], a commercial bank must consider the availability of alternative service providers or the possibility of bringing the outsourced activity back in-house in an emergency, along with the costs, time, and resources involved. [S1] specifies that these factors are essential for establishing a viable contingency plan.

According to [S1] para 11, the Board or a Committee of the Board to which powers have been delegated is responsible for putting in place a framework to evaluate the risks and materiality of all existing and prospective outsourcing arrangements.

Yes, the RBI outsourcing requirements apply to subcontracted activities. As stated in [S1], paragraph 4(2), the bank must obtain prior approval or consent before the service provider engages any subcontractor, and must review the subcontracting arrangement to ensure it complies with Chapter III Directions.

According to [S1], commercial banks shall not outsource core management functions including Internal Audit, the compliance function, and decision-making functions such as determining compliance with KYC norms for opening deposit accounts, giving sanction for loans (including retail loans), and management of investment portfolio.

A bank must establish a risk management framework that comprehensively addresses the identification, measurement, mitigation, management, and reporting of risks from IT outsourcing arrangements [S1]. Additionally, it must have a management structure to monitor and control outsourced services, including performance, uptime, service availability, SLA adherence, and incident response mechanisms [S2].
